entry.content:
Issue #68 of befores & afters magazine covers the visual effects of The End of Oak Street.

DIGITAL MAGAZINE members can download the issue right now from the shop post.

David Robert Mitchell, the filmmaker behind It Follows (2014) and Under the Silver Lake (2018), takes a decidedly different approach to science-fiction adventure with The End of Oak Street. Set in 1982, the film follows the Platt family—Denise (Anne Hathaway), Greg (Ewan McGregor) and their children Audrey (Maisy Stella) and Brian (Christian Convery)—whose already complicated family life is thrown into extraordinary circumstances when a mysterious cosmic event tears their suburban Michigan neighborhood from its surroundings and transports it millions of years into the past. What was once a quiet residential street is suddenly surrounded by prehistoric wilderness, with the inhabitants discovering that they are no longer at the top of the food chain.

As the neighborhood struggles to understand what has happened, the Platts find themselves facing an increasingly dangerous collection of prehistoric creatures, including dinosaurs that roam between the houses and surrounding forests. The production combined location shooting, practical stunt work and extensive visual effects to create the film’s unusual collision of familiar suburbia and prehistoric wilderness.

The substantial digital effects workload was handled by Industrial Light & Magic, which delivered approximately 700 visual effects shots across its Sydney, San Francisco and Vancouver facilities. The work encompassed several prehistoric species, including an Allosaurus, Coelophysis, Camarasaurus and the enormous Titanoboa, as well as digital doubles, extensive environment extensions and the transformation of the neighborhood into a prehistoric landscape.

In this special issue of befores & afters magazine, we dive into The End of Oak Street’s effects work with production visual effects supervisor Jay Cooper (who hails from ILM), ILM visual effects supervisor Trevor Hazel, and special effects supervisor J.D. Schwalm. They discuss the work in their own words, accompanied by a range of behind the scenes imagery.

entry.title: Behind the tools and techniques used to craft those subtle facial enhancements in ‘Obsession’
entry.summary: Visual effects supervisor Peter Timberlake discusses his Plastik toolset. In Curry Barker’s Obsession , Bear (Michael Johnston) is a hopeless romantic who, after failing to express his feelings for childhood friend Nikki (Inde Navarrette), breaks a mysterious novelty item called
entry.content:
Visual effects supervisor Peter Timberlake discusses his Plastik toolset.

In Curry Barker’s Obsession, Bear (Michael Johnston) is a hopeless romantic who, after failing to express his feelings for childhood friend Nikki (Inde Navarrette), breaks a mysterious novelty item called the One Wish Willow and wishes that she would love him more than anyone in the world. When the wish comes true, Nikki is cursed, and her affection quickly develops into a frightening, uncontrollable obsession, transforming Bear’s romantic fantasy into a nightmare.

Obsessive facial expressions made by Nikki during the film reach unsettling levels. A mix of practical make-up and 2D compositing techniques aided in pushing Navarrette’s impressive performance even further into a deliberate Uncanny Valley. Importantly, the visual effects enhancements were of the invisible variety, remaining as only subtle shifts to the actor’s facial features. 

Here, befores & afters talks to production visual effects supervisor Peter Timberlake about the tools and techniques his studio, Queen, relied upon to craft those subtle facial augmentations. He also mentions other VFX-related work in the film, ranging from a unique approach to previs, the blood and gore enhancements, and a completely undetectable visual effects shot for the final scene. 

Uncanny Valley: the facial enhancements brief

Timberlake shares with befores & afters the initial brief to Queen for the facial augmentation shots: “Curry wanted to push Nikki into the Uncanny Valley without much elaboration on what pixels needed to go where, but rather just the impression that the audience needed to get when they came across Nikki. As visual effects artists, we just tried stuff to see what Curry reacted to. Our early tests started with us taking stills, as well as full shots, of Nikki’s face and modifying them and running them by Curry and seeing what he thought.”

“I think what I didn’t fully realize at the time,” adds Timberlake, “is how thorough the theme of the Uncanny Valley runs through Obsession, through every department. Even down to how the script is written, where Curry wrote scenes where Nikki is hot and cold, where she’s saying how much she loves him, and then in the next breath is totally angry at him. It’s not the Uncanny Valley in the traditional sense, but it gives you this weird destabilizing effect where you don’t really know what’s in her mind.”

An example of a scene that helped Timberlake understand this move into the Uncanny Valley was the first interaction Bear has with the obsessed Nikki. “Curry shot it two ways, one where Nikki was into Bear and another where she was totally friend-zoning Bear. And then he intercut those takes so that the audience, shot-to-shot, is feeling, ‘Oh, she’s into him,’ and ‘Oh, she’s not into him.’ I think that the ambiguity and lack of knowing there gives it that Uncanny Valley effect. Curry also mentioned that he had given Nikki a line where she said that her cat died and her cat didn’t die, but Bear’s cat did die in the film. Curry said that that kind of half-truth was his extrapolation of the Uncanny Valley theme into a character’s line. Curry wanted to build out this Uncanny Valley-type of philosophy into the visuals of the film.”

The idea was all about dualism. You see that throughout the movie—there’s all these famous shots of her smiling and saying, ‘No, no, no, no.’ Or the shot where she’s frowning, and gets a laugh from the audience. We wanted to give the audience two emotions at once. One, the emotion that her muscles convey, and two, the opposite ‘gut feeling’ that is being conveyed. There was even a brief that Curry gave the make-up team that was: ‘Paint kind of like a smiling Kabuki-style puppet make-up onto her, but her actual face is going to be frowning.’” 

For the enhancements, Timberlake admits that he thought the director was initially looking to add a more ‘feral’ look to Nikki. “It was a look that we’ve probably seen in a handful of movies. I think V/H/S is my favorite example of a more feral look that is definitely Uncanny Valley. But that look is more like the character’s been raised by wolves, and not what Curry was going for. We did try that and ran it by Curry and he was like, ‘Why don’t we try doing basically the opposite of what you’ve just done here?’”

“He did not want the eyes to be really big,” adds Timberlake. “He didn’t want the features and the performance to be exaggerated. We wanted them to be almost mismatched and done in the opposite direction. So when her eyes are really big, we want to make them really small. And when her mouth is smiling, we want to tilt it down. What this actually achieved in the end was communicating a mixed message, where you feel that there’s one Nikki that’s the obsessed Nikki, and then there’s this trapped Nikki underneath who is frowning while smiling or smiling while frowning, or something that would be impossible for an actor to do without the unintentional visual philosophy behind it.”

The Plastik toolset

To tackle the facial enhancement shots for Obsession, Timberlake and his team at Queen worked within their proprietary toolkit called Plastik. “It’s built primarily within Nuke, and then a handful of other tools that we have written scripts around in order to get them all into Nuke. That’s mostly because Nuke is where our final comps are coming from and what the artists are familiar with. Originally we had used it for an earlier project where there was a CG thing that was on a character’s skin and it was not lining up. We used this tool to pin little pieces of skin so that the transform was diffused across a large area, making the skin and the CG elements stick. The underlying technology was then transferable to all different types of skin and features that have perspective shifts. It lets us work in screen space once and have the transformation survive through perspective shifts and changes in performance.”

Timberlake acknowledges that typically for facial augmentation work, you might normally head down a geometry tracked-based workflow. But since this was a low-budget film, it was determined that geometry tracks were not the desired approach. Instead, a 2D workflow with Plastik / Nuke was utilized. Here’s how a facial enhancement shot was carried out.

“As an artist,” explains Timberlake, “you would be working on one frame and getting that one frame right. The controls are the same as the transform node controls in Nuke, but you can choose what area of the face you’re transforming and how that falls off. On a typical shot, we would probably be using six to 12 layers of transforms where we’re focusing on left eye bottom, right eye bottom, left eye side, right eye side, mouth, etc etc. After you get it done in one frame, it typically will track throughout both the performance and through perspective shifts in her face. That enabled us to do a pretty large amount of work without relying on geometry tracks, which have a lot of upstream dependencies and make computers run slower and just make the pipeline crunch a little bit more.”

Timberlake continues on the process: “After the initial tracking step is done, we can be very, very flexible. I remember once I was actually on the phone with Curry. I pulled up a shot and over a screenshare, I was just pulling and pushing stuff around, We went from, ‘This is wrong’ to ‘This is awesome’ in probably five minutes. Obviously that was on one frame and we had to make sure that that frame worked across the entire shot, but that was a cool experience to be like, ‘I can do a real-time session with a director using this toolkit.’”

It was a learning curve for Timberlake to work out exactly what the director was after, but ultimately extremely subtle augmentations were settled upon. “I think that our first rounds to Curry were more noticeable, partly because we had made an assumption, not really being that familiar with Curry’s work, that he was just another genre filmmaker who was making low-budget horror movies and he wanted to shock everyone with this character. And it turned out that he was going for something a lot more nuanced and he told us to basically dial it back quite a bit. And because of that, I think that the effect is a lot more successful.”

Not previs, but lightvis

Director of photography Taylor Clemons planned out scenes in the film by previsualizing moments with Unreal Engine. But, says Timberlake, it was not in the usual ‘previs’ sense. “He did previs specifically designed for lighting and blocking. It’s something I’ve called ‘lightvis’. I think without this tool, Obsession would probably have been impossible. I mean, Curry and Taylor together spent hours in the software—there was a little log of the time they spent in there and it was thousands of hours. They would first import a LiDAR scan of the actual locations and then they’d put in lights and characters and move cameras around. The idea was, it basically gives you a menu of every ingredient that you have at your disposal. It gave them time to find the movie.” 

 

“With Unreal Engine and all the accurate real-world lights in there,” continues Timberlake, “you can get a pretty close result before you step foot on set. And then when you go onto set, you’re feeling a lot more prepared and ready to be with the actor instead of having to figure out all of the logistics. And you’re giving your Grip & Electric crew all of this data that says, ‘Here’s what we’re going for. This light goes here and this light goes here.’ It means we don’t have to spend all this time messing with lights and figuring out the look of the scene. It’s something that any young filmmaker can do, or frankly any seasoned filmmaker can do, too. I think it makes these small budget features a lot more viable as long as the artistic vision is there from the beginning.”

The lightvis process came in handy, too, for some LED wall shooting that was used for filming car scenes. “Credit goes to Taylor on this, again,” says Timberlake. “We used pre-shot footage rather than Unreal Engine footage on the LED wall. I think the end shots worked so well because they are dark and are lit the same way that he would light anything else. Taylor seems to understand that just because it’s an LED wall, it doesn’t mean that all of your cinematography rules go out the window. He did a few clever things, one of which was make the windows really dirty and smudgy and it gives you this interactivity between the talent, the midground set—which in this case is a car in most cases—and then the actual lights on set, that filters the LED wall through this layer that almost simmers it into something that all feels locked together.”

Classic horror effects

Since Obsession is a horror movie, Queen was called upon to enhance a few moments of blood and gore. One moment sees Nikki smash a character’s head into a brick placed on a car steering wheel. “For the head smash,” outlines Timberlake, “the approach was to take a performance of a test dummy, which was a prosthetic of the actress, and then to use a take of the actress and basically extract textures from each of them and blend them together as the take goes on. So, we took the real actress’s face, put it on the test dummy, then we took gore elements from the test dummy and put it on the real actress’ face. For each consecutive hit, it progresses from the real actress to the full gore test dummy.”

Smaller visual effects augmentations related to blood and gore included dealing with a character being shot and removing some blood tubing. Another kind of horror effect Queen worked on required close collaboration with the editing of certain scenes, as Timberlake breaks down. “In his temp edit, Curry had done a lot of these smash cuts. So, we’d go from one performance of a character with a bottle, bringing it to their head, and not hitting their head, and then the next frame is them doing a separate take where they do the reaction. He had intentionally cut a few frames to make it look more sudden. In our first few versions, we had made it more natural, without the missing frames. But Curry asked us to keep it without the frames. My interpretation of that was that he wanted it to look a little more horror genre-y, and lean into the genre, or it could be that he just fell in love with his original edit. Either way, audiences seemed to like it.” 

That end shot

Spoiler alert: the film ends with Bear’s character dying on Nikki’s lap, which releases Nikki from the curse. A lengthy shot required some completely invisible effects intervention. 

“In the take, they were coming off some intense action and the actor was breathing heavily. Well, since it was massively important that the character is not breathing,” points out Timberlake, “we were asked to make his chest still—which sounds easy and I thought would be easy at first—but the problem is that Nikki is messing with his body and his shirt a lot, so we had to retain all of the motion that was related to her, while stabilizing the underlying motion. It turned into a really challenging shot that was also very long and one we can’t really brag about. You can’t say on your reel, ‘Look at how this character isn’t doing something!’ It’s the quintessential ‘can’t put it on your reel’ shot. But it was central to the plot, to show that this character wasn’t breathing.”

entry.content:
The film tells the story of Tenzing Norgay and his historic 1953 summit of Mount Everest alongside Edmund Hillary.

The film’s visual effects supervisor was Jay Hawkins, who provided befores & afters with this note about the production:

On Tenzing, visual effects worked as a production partner from early preproduction. With a full Everest shoot too dangerous at altitude, the climb was captured in New Zealand’s Southern Alps and rebuilt as the real mountain across 630 largely invisible shots, drawn from real plates and a library of over 34,000 Everest images.

VFX supervisor: Jay Hawkins
VFX producer: Octavia Mansfield
VFX vendors: ARC, Alt.VFX, Blackbird, Future Associate, Alussein

entry.title: Stop-motion delights
entry.summary: The making of stop-motion animated Arges and Bullethead by Tippett Studio, including some Star Wars-related Easter eggs to look out for. An excerpt from issue #68 of the magazine. In Star Wars history, Phil Tippett is a key player in the creation of so many pivotal characters, ve
entry.content:
The making of stop-motion animated Arges and Bullethead by Tippett Studio, including some Star Wars-related Easter eggs to look out for. An excerpt from issue #68 of the magazine.

In Star Wars history, Phil Tippett is a key player in the creation of so many pivotal characters, vehicles and sequences, especially in terms of stop-motion and puppet work. Memorable Tippett moments relate to the Dejarik holochess game, Tauntauns, walkers and the Rancor. His Tippett Studio has, in more recent times, been brought on board the Star Wars streaming series to contribute stop-motion animation (for the Trash Walkers in The Mandalorian series, B’omarr monks in The Book of Boba Fett and Mama Crab in Skeleton Crew). For The Mandalorian and Grogu, Tippett Studio realized the robotic Hutt Palace guards.

“We knew in pre-production we wanted to do a sequence with Tippett,” shares Knoll. “The thing that stood out to me as relatively contained that was a really good choice was the Mando and Grogu fight with those droids. It’s about two minutes long. It’s 36 shots. So it was kind of on the ambitious end, with two fairly complex characters. They’re multi-limbed. Each one of them has three arms and they have all these moving pieces on them; moving parts on their heads, moving armor plates, and this moving skirt. In fact, the Tippett guys said it was the most complicated thing that they’ve ever done, and it took a better part of a year to shoot.”

“Part of Jon Favreau’s feeling is that stop-motion has a charm to it,” adds Knoll. “It’s okay that you can tell it’s stop-motion, in the same way that it’s okay you’re looking at a puppet or a guy in a rubber mask. That’s always been part of Star Wars and part of the suspension of disbelief and what people like about them.”

The clear ‘look and feel’ of classic staccato stop-motion animation is all throughout the droid fight, but motion blur was added to the final shots. “The live-action with Mando running around has motion blur,” notes Knoll. “And when the camera pans, there’s motion blur in that. We didn’t want to have completely crisp still frames. So, we’d do an optical flow-based motion blur over the top of the stop-motion to try and get it to be this hybrid aesthetic that’s partly between Harryhausen back in the day, and what you see in computer graphics, that is, somewhere in that spectrum where the motion blur isn’t all technically accurate. There’s places where it’s a little clipped or isn’t exactly right, but it’s not quite as jarring of an aesthetic difference as the old Harryhausen stuff is.”

Tippett Studio was engaged early to help figure out what some of the fun gags could be featuring the droid guards. “We started by basically asking Phil to dream up stuff, to just give us his thoughts,” recalls Hickel. “He went away for a little bit, came back some point later and had some rough boards he’d done. They had cut them together with some music just so he could pitch them to Jon Favreau. It then became a combination of what was in the script, Phil’s ideas, and other storyboards by Dave Lowery. We would effectively have little story meetings. It would be me and the editors and John Knoll and Jon Favreau and his writing partner Noah Kloor, as well as Doug Chiang and the whole brains trust down in LA. We would talk through the sequence and the ideas and work it out.”

Early CG previs and rough animation was also explored. “We were trying desperately to avoid having to do retakes on things that were this complicated,” suggests Knoll. “We wanted to make sure that everybody was buying into the shot designs and the timings and that the storytelling was all working for everybody, so that when it came time to do these tremendously labor-intensive animations, that, to the largest extent possible, we were only doing a single take on each one.”

At Tippett Studio, individual artists took on multiple roles for the stop-motion guards, from fabrication to animation and photography. “This work is definitely an extension of what we’ve been doing already,” mentions Tippett Studio visual effects supervisor Ken Rogerson. “Every show in the Star Wars franchise is just a little more elaborate than the last.”

After the ideation process with Phil Tippett, artists at the studio continued to work with Doug Chiang on droid designs. “Doug wanted us to go back and forth a little bit with their art department to build out the droids,” establishes Tippett Studio visual effects supervisor Mark Dubeau. “They came to us kind of bare bones with not a lot of detailing on the designs. We had an opportunity to not only add more detail, but we had to modify them as we were building them so that they actually worked with the stop-motion armature inside. It was a good thing that they hadn’t gone too far with them because there might’ve been a bunch of detail we would’ve had to eradicate while we were figuring out how to fit the armature inside and all of that.”

This early stage also involved continual back and forth with the filmmakers. Tippett Studio then crafted its own CG versions of the droids. “Ultimately,” explains Hickel, “they were going to do a lot of 3D printing for all the super complicated parts. So they built full CG versions of these droids and rigged them to be animated in Maya. They had all the detail, but on layers it had the planned armature and how all the pieces fit and everything.”

That process continued into Tippett Studio previs’ing the sequence itself. “They had done this with the Mama Crab where they pre-animated in CG so that folks could buy off on speed and timing and choreography before they dove into the hard work,” says Hickel. “It was a lengthy process of them generating CG previs in Maya. I would also be generating previs. Tippett gave me their CG assets, and I was cooking up shots and ideas in my spare time. I’d cut stuff together, I’d hand stuff to our editor Dylan, the editor, he’d cut stuff. We’d show it to Jon Favreau, he’d have a bunch of notes and we’d do that cycle over. We did it over and over and over again ahead of shooting that scene until we finally got to a sequence where we could all say, ‘Yeah, this is what it is.’”

Tippett Studio visual effects supervisor Tom ‘Gibby’ Gibbons reiterates why that long previs process was necessary. “The way that the schedule works, it’s very different in visual effects than it is in an actual animated film. We have to establish what everything is and what they do before we ever get to the stage and to shooting them. We’ve been super lucky with the Star Wars series that all the directors seem to really get it and they don’t fight it and they don’t push back and get annoyed. It’s like they look at this as part of the, ‘Yeah, we’re figuring this out and as we go,’ and it works out really great that way.”

Once the previs had been agreed upon, live-action for the fight was filmed (second unit director Peter Ramsey directed the sequence). “They went onto a soundstage and shot Mando against a bluescreen,” states Rogerson, “knowing what the action was and where his eyeline would be and how far he had to run in every shot so they could get plates that then would interact with the robots when we went back and shot those stop-motion.”

The next step was puppet fabrication of the two droids, which ended up being dubbed Bullethead and Argus (more on why, later). One of Tippett Studio’s challenges in the build related to the robot nature of the droids, made up of more than 60 individual pieces each. “All the pieces that were eventually kit bashed together had to be created into something that could be solidly printed and then interact with each other,” details Tippett Studio lead fabricator John ‘JD’ Daniel. “These were hard surfaces, these weren’t soft puppets. Again, that’s why having that previs was essential because we needed to know things like, is the droid going to be reaching very far above his head? If that’s the case, where’s that shoulder going to go, and how does that all interact? Every single piece of these droids becomes a small engineering project to make sure that it fits on the armature that we’re designing while the animation is being figured out.”

Tippett Studio’s Brett Foxwell custom-built a steel armature, some of which deliberately shows through the droids outer shell. “You can actually see a lot of the actual real metal of the armature in there, which was really fun to do for this droid,” states Daniel. “Other parts were made to look like an armature, but it’s really 3D printed resin. There’s also a whole lot of parts that were done with the traditional process of mold making and casting.”

The droids were ultimately made out of a number of materials: steel, resin, silicone, urethane, wire and even rubber bands. “You name it, everything came into play,” shares Dubeau. “John Favreau was really picky about the paint scheme on these things, too. He had a lot of rules in terms of the colors that could be beside each other. If we had the wrong green and red next to each other, he would just go, ‘Boba Fett! That looks like Boba Fett. So I’d have to completely repaint it and make it a different color.”

The droids were designed to feature skirts. “Originally they had skirts that were cloth,” mentions Dubeau. “We were banging our heads trying to figure out, okay, well, how can we do this? Gibby actually has experience animating a cloth and he suggested putting these pieces of flexible material behind the skirts.”

“Yes,” adds Daniel, “Gibby made these little pieces of styrene to look like rusted metal. And in the end, we came up with these neat metal chimes like plates hanging down. At first we tried wire attachments, but wire has a ‘memory’ which turned out to inhibit really granular movement where one blade would touch another. So we opted for each of them having a ball and socket.”

“They were a nightmare to make,” reveals Gibbons, “but what was really funny is they weren’t as much of a nightmare as they looked like because there was a rhythm to them that it was almost comforting compared to the rest of them because once I started animating shots, I could just move one and then every other one cascaded behind it. It just turns into this rhythm when you’re doing the shot. The only time that it got messy was when a leg would move forward or they’d twist and all of a sudden, the plates would pinch and you’d have to predict that before you got there so you could start trying to move them behind each other or in front of each other so they’d stack instead of collide.”

In fact, Dubeau admits that Tippett Studio “tried for a little bit to convince John Knoll and his team to take on those plates as a digital element, but I think that we did the right thing. I know that people wanted to be able to point at it and go, ‘That’s all stop-motion.’ The only thing that’s not stop-motion coming out of them is really their laser blasts and a hand grenade. Everything else is pretty much in-camera.”

The in-camera nature of the fight included almost everything seen behind the droids, with the environment in which they were animated being a miniature set that had to match the full-scale live-action one. “The environment was a big undertaking,” discusses Dubeau. “In the Hutt Palace, you’re basically going through mycelium, you’re in a giant spore. The idea is that these are all bubbles inside of oxygen or whatever it is that gets caught in there and they’ve essentially drilled through them. So that’s why everything was incredibly curved and linear and almost perfect. That was actually very challenging to get these super clean and pleasing shapes because initially, we were looking at it and it’s like, oh, it’s like a cave. And when we got the concept art for it and the lines were so clean, I thought that it would end up rough-looking, but it didn’t.”

“We had to explain to the miniature set builders, ‘It’s like going in with a giant melon baller and just scooping these perfect circles out,’” continues Dubeau. “I remember walking onto the stage and Kayte Sabicer and Bill Boes were in there and they were just sanding these very sweeping arcs to get those perfect round things. Just the looks on their faceS because it goes against what you really want to do. You want to make things really rough. But of course it looked great on screen and it really matched what they had done on set.”

The doors in front of which the droids stand guard brought their own set of complications. The original idea was that they were doors to the Hutt throne room, and so were built very clean. “We made these beautiful bronze, gold and silver doors,” explains Dubeau. “There was a little tarnish to them and then Jon Favreau saw them and said, ‘No, I want to see rust and all this stuff.’ I would be just sitting there for day after day after day, just adding more rust, putting it on set, taking a picture, sending it to him and he’s like, ‘No, more, more.’ But that’s the fun part. You always want to hear ‘more, more’ because the moment they start saying, ‘Oh, less, less,’ it’s really hard to take stuff away.”

The choice to animate the droids in a set rather than against a greenscreen, say, was driven by the desired end look, according to Rogerson. “Especially because this is a very much a pools of light kind of environment and a lot of interactive light when the explosions are going off, especially with any reflective surfaces on the robot. If you shoot it on greenscreen, you’re always going to be fighting that comp look. If you’re really careful about how you light things, you can get there, but by doing it the way we did it, you’re going to get it so much faster and you’re going to get so much more detail.”

“One of the things that you always find with environments is that if you want a nice, beautiful cityscape of a futuristic city with clean glass, you can do that in a computer,” adds Rogerson. “But if you want a grungy, damp, dirty cave, it’s going to be faster to do that by throwing dirt on a wall and gluing some roots to plaster. You’re going to get so much more detail and realism out of that. Especially if you’re working with people that have experience with miniatures. It’s going to have the right scale and it’s just going to look fantastic and you don’t have to question whether you’ve done the right thing to make it look real because it is real. For example, we might paint things with shellac to get that puddle of water look and make everything look damp. It certainly was a lot of work to build that set. Obviously, we were on it for months, but man-hours wise, to do that as a digital environment would’ve probably been more and then would’ve had that digital curse to it that you never quite get around.”

“The reason it goes faster in the real world is you get your detritus for free,” suggests Gibbons. “You get the dust you can’t get out of the nooks and crannies, the sawdust, just the grime that becomes part of the world because you literally couldn’t scrub it out if you wanted to. And that’s the 10% that in a CG world, it’s actually really hard to do convincingly without making it look very artificially placed or repetitively made through some scatter system.”

The miniature set was lit with the aid of cucoloris boards, also known as kooks. Explains Gibbons: “It’s a very small pattern of sticks or tape and you put it in front of a light. This is the thing that we get in the real world. I’ve seen people try to do this digitally and it’s really hard and takes a lot of smart people working on CG lights, noise patterns or shader responses, or interference channels, and I’m not convinced it always works. In stop-motion you can use some ‘toothpicks, tape and hot glue’ and you get the same thing. But as the characters just move gently even through light like that, it breaks their spec patterns up. It just creates this slight fade undulation in highlights. A lot of modulation that’s super granular, almost like you wouldn’t see it. You’d have to stare at it to see it, but if it wasn’t there, that’s what makes things look like plastic and not like a real thing. All those sorts of tricks that we know about in each one of our little eccentric little arts are the reason why this stuff will end up looking real. It looks like stop-motion, but it looks real.”

Adds Gibbons: “Here is a fun factoid. One of the reasons our small band works so well together, I have always used kooks, but it was Ken who really explained why we do them, because he was putting kook designs on bounce cards and I was like, ‘Come on, man, we gotta get this shot launched,’ and he explained fully why he was, so I learned something new and didn’t ever bug him again about putting interference kooks anywhere he wanted them.”

Painting the droids required special attention to detail, notes Dubeau. “If you paint something to be silvery and then you put it on film, depending on the lights, it can wind up just looking gray. Doug Chiang wanted to feel like there were a lot of high kicks off the metal. Now, there’s not that much real metal on it. So what I had to do is figure out the right kind of paints, especially at that scale, for things to come to life. You almost have to paint everything with chrome paint so that you get those pings. The risk is that it can make it look really, really big because it’ll get a sharp, hot little ping. And as he’s moving through these cucoloris lights, the sheen on it, it’ll dance and you’ll get that. It’ll trick your eye into thinking it’s this really big thing.”

The puppets were rigged with internal lights, handled by Tippett Studio stage manager Blair Mendel. Says Rogerson: “Blair wired up all of the LEDs and figured out how to balance the brightness of all those and make the wires disappear. He also built all of the rigs for the interactive lighting because every time they shoot their gun or an explosion goes off, then there’s an interactive light pass that we’ve shot so that they cast their shadow on the wall behind them and each other.”

The droids were constantly being touched up during the stop-motion shoot. “I would fully paint them, put them on stage and within about three, four shots we’re having to take it off-stage and then I’m going in and doing touch-ups again,” recounts Dubeau. “Every shot I would have to go in with my little triage kit. They’re really manhandling these things so paint is going to rub off. As much as I would love them to animate wearing gloves, it’s just not practical. Also, any time I’d see a bag of popcorn on the set, I’d throw it in the garbage. I’d say, ‘No salt, no salt.’ It attacks the paint like crazy.”

Daniel was called in only a few times for fixes. “There were actually a few times where something was either about to break or had broken in a shot and there was some in-between frame surgery that had to happen, but it was very rare,” he says.

Animation of the droids was handled primarily by Gibbons and Chuck Duke, with David Lauer and Ri Crawford also contributing. The large loose-jointed builds of the puppets suited the desired motion, being deliberately mechanical and jittery. Gibbons gave the larger of the droids somewhat of a ‘Frankenstein’ motion by leaning him forward—a suggestion from Phil Tippett—as he worked on walk cycles.

The area was tight to animate in. “We only had one of each puppet,” remarks Gibbons. “So while they were on-screen together, there could only be one animator because animating on a set that’s a cave, you can’t get two animators in there, and you can only get one guy in there at a time. So, that was just me animating all the shots where they’re together. Then as soon as we could cut that set in half, we could use the second animator which was Chuck, who is amazing.”

Hickel, who had previously been a stop-motion animator at Will Vinton Studios, lent his services to animate a shot, too—“It was the easiest shot in the sequence!” Hickel offers (the shot involved one of the droids coming to life with its ‘eye’ spinning around and lighting up). Gibbons remarks, “On every show, I think I’ve said to Hal, ‘You’ve got to come shoot a shot.’ And he’s like, ‘Well, I don’t know, I don’t know.’ And he finally came in for this one and I was so excited because Hal’s no slouch either. He’s really good. So, to get him to come down and just touch a puppet again was so great. Chuck and Hal have known each other since Will Vinton days.”

At this animation stage, one issue the team came up against was that the puppets did not hold themselves up without a supporting rig. There were other challenges, too, as Gibbons outlines. “One of the things that we all learned scientifically, or at least I did, is that the difference between static friction and kinetic friction is very different. Even when you’ve got characters like this, when you want to start moving them after they’ve sat there having their frame taken, the static friction is so strong to overcome, you basically have to just lean into it to get them moving, but it would push them way past the tiny increment you wanted so then you were pulling them back and then pushing them forward and so on and so on until they magically land where you wanted them in the first place.”

Mando’s miniatures, puppets, stop-motion and more

“I started to call it ‘shake animation’,” continues Gibbons, “because once the static friction was overcome I’d just sit there and shake the puppet trying to let it not seize up again until I got it where I wanted, almost like with a baseball bat. Well, that wasn’t going to work for the show. So, Ken and I came up with different kinds of character rigs that we could use and sneak into the scene. Brett Foxwell came up a fantastic system of handles and rig ports we could access depending on where the camera was. We could shove them into the back of the droids to help hold them up and then I could loosen the armature just enough that the static friction wasn’t as much of a problem.”

“Beyond that,” says Gibbons, “I had some helper rigs, one in particular called a machinist jack. They’re super precise and very strong and I would use those and then I would use wood blocks/shims. I’m still dying for somebody watching the film to go, ‘Is that wood underneath their feet?’ Because as they take a step I literally would stack wood underneath their feet so that as they take a step forward, the foot would rise and fall, and they’d still be standing on a ground plane, and then I would start pulling it out. We also came up with these ‘don’t touch them’ handles that I would put into the top and into the bottoms so that I could move the whole body without touching the body. And then once I got it to where I wanted, I’d pull those handles out and then I could manipulate elbows, legs, little bits and pieces. These were the most difficult puppets I’ve ever had to control.”

Interestingly, the Tippett Studio team found they were initially nervous at having their work be seen on large cinema screens, including IMAX. “We just really wanted to make sure that it was going to look good,” remembers Daniel. “We actually asked ILM if we could play a couple of tests of our work in one of their big screening rooms. And so they invited us up and we got to go and take a look and it was really satisfying to be able to be like, ‘Oh yeah, we can do this.’”

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by bfophoto (@bfophoto)

“That was a good moment,” notes Dubeau, “because everybody went to that room, I think, a little bit sheepishly. Because even when we were detailing it, I was putting some stuff in there, we’d print it out and I’d look at it and I’d be like, ‘Oh, that’s not detailed enough. I need to go further.’ I would put these little screws in the model and then when the thing printed out, they’re not even a millimeter in diameter. They’re these tiny little things. But then when I look at them on the screen, they’re like the size of Oreo cookies. They’re really, really big!”

“I always had faith in what we were doing,” laughs Rogerson. “The beauty of doing things for real is that you get that infinite detail. This is something we’ve all learned from Phil Tippett. He’s the master of this: rust it up, spray acid on it, glue on a bunch of dirt, and then shoot it dark and you can get away with just absolute murder and you get this sense that there’s a real object there without having to put a lot of thought and effort into it.”

The names Bullethead and Arges for the droids were dreamt up by Tippett Studio. “They came to us as ‘Giant Droid A’ and ‘Giant Droid B,’’ reveals Daniel. “Us being the crew that we are, we’re like, ‘Well, we need to give them names.’ So, B became Bullethead for perhaps for the logically obvious reason to match his head shape. Then Mark named Arges after one of the three Greek cyclopees. And now that’s Star Wars canon.”

While the final result was incredibly pleasing to the Tippett Studio team, they are more than happy to share some war stories during the process. “There was a great shot where Arges falls to his knees,” recalls Gibbons. “Well, the armature was such that they could only bend forward at a 45 degree angle and then the whole thing locked up. So I basically had to suspend the rig and unscrew, at first, the toes, and then the heels of the feet and then through the armature that was exposed at that point, stick wires through those so that they wouldn’t slide around and drill two holes, stick the wires through to hold the ankle or the bottom of the shin to the floor and then take the feet in two pieces on each side and try to get them to look like they were folding under and going backwards. Big plastic metal parts couldn’t do that. So then I sculpted them out of clay and replaced the real ones with clay, bent them backwards and then put the real feet back in again. I challenge you to find that in the show! The only thing that I was missing was drawing a picture of a foot and sticking it back there.”

Mando’s miniatures, puppets, stop-motion and more

Gibbons also remembers a time when they were assembling Arges for a shot and forgot to add his side strap. “There’s this big leather plate that holds the straps together and somehow, it had gotten taken off so we could get to the armature. We just did a whole shot without it. Mark, being the art director, was beside himself. But I was like, ‘Yeah, nobody’s going to see it. It’s in the shadows.’ I actually can’t find the shot it’s missing in! I love little Easter eggs like that, like on the rare occasion where Harryhausen would leave a surface gauge in for one frame. It’s kinda nerdy fun to find little signs of the ‘hand behind the curtain’ on things like that.

Then there are the Easter eggs the team was able to include. Bullethead’s club that he swings as a weapon is one to look out for, suggests Daniel. “Mark made all these designs for the club, all of them really cool. And then for one of them was, he took a weapon from one of the original Star Wars Kenner action figures. It was the Lando Calrissian in Skiff Guard disguise. He had this little vibro-ax which Mark took and duplicated four times, and it was approved!”

“I just put it in there,” says Dubeau. “It was a stupid gag. If you look at the club and then you look at the vibro-ax, I just took the blade off the ax, then just put it around four times, and it’s almost completely unadulterated from the toy version. John Favreau was like, ‘I want that.’ I was really surprised. We called it the vibro-club.”

Another Easter egg relates to Bullethead’s belt buckle. For the Mama Crab we had little R2-D2s stuck in different areas,” mentions Dubeau. “Well, when we got Bullethead, he didn’t have a belt or anything like that. He just had a skirt that went around. And then as we progressed the design, they decided they wanted to have this rack of grenades on a belt. So, I designed a belt that worked a little bit like a conveyor belt. What I realized then was that we needed a belt buckle. Anybody who’s a big fan of Star Wars and pays attention to all the greebles that get put on a model ship, well, I chose something for the belt buckle, which is a very well known model piece used in a ton of stuff on Star Wars shows.”

“Hopefully, the fans that were watching it did one of those Leonardo DiCaprio point-at-the-screen memes when they saw it, because there’s this one shot where you see the grenade come around and he grabs it and the belt buckle is right there. I can’t do one of these projects without putting in a little Easter egg or two.”

entry.title: A visual journey through the miniatures of ‘Digger’
entry.summary: Miniature supervisor Simon Weisse breaks down the model builds for the film. In director Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Digger , Tom Cruise stars as Digger Rockwell, a powerful oil magnate whose reckless pursuit of fossil fuels unleashes an environmental catastrophe that threatens to de
entry.content:
Miniature supervisor Simon Weisse breaks down the model builds for the film.

In director Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Digger, Tom Cruise stars as Digger Rockwell, a powerful oil magnate whose reckless pursuit of fossil fuels unleashes an environmental catastrophe that threatens to devastate the planet. As the disaster unfolds, Digger embarks on a frantic mission to convince the world that he is humanity’s saviour.

Well, that’s what the film appears to be about. Without going into too many spoilers here, one of the ways the film’s distinctive, deliberately artificial visual world was brought to life was through an extensive combination of physical miniatures and dioramas—which become story points themselves—that were augmented with practical special effects and digital visual effects, blending traditional filmmaking techniques with contemporary VFX.

Miniature supervisor Simon Weisse oversaw a diverse array of miniatures for the film which were built in his Berlin studio and transported to Pinewood Studios in the UK for filming. Here he talks to befores & afters about how the miniatures work came together. 

How miniatures became part of the film

Weisse recounts the call he received from Digger producer Michael Sharp, who relayed that ‘Alejandro wants miniatures’. “Michael and I had worked together previously and said, ‘Could you come to London next week?’ I went there to Leavesden Studios where they have made some test setups. They had very simple miniatures made by the art department, which did fantastic work in a very short time, but they were just tests. I was there with Alejandro, and the DOP Emmanuel Lubezki, Chivo. It’s tough with these very famous people in front of you! One thing was, they wanted to play with real water in the miniatures. I said, ‘No, you can’t do this. It doesn’t work.’ It was very difficult saying no to Alejandro Iñárritu, but when I said no, from that moment I think they respected me.”

The filmmakers then said to Weisse, he recalls, “‘Well, how would you do it?’ I said, ‘We could mix our traditional techniques with new technologies. Why don’t you do the water in CG? It works much better and will be much more believable.’ I suggested we could do certain landscapes and elements as miniatures, then scan them, and put them into a 3D environment. In the end, it worked well because the artists from Industrial Light & Magic, they were very open to model making and to miniatures in general. So that became our approach, where we would also incorporate practical effects from special effects supervisor Dominic Tuohy.” 

First miniature: the nature vista

Weisse’s team in Berlin began work firstly on what they called the ‘nature vista’ miniature. “It’s that huge landscape with the river in the middle,” shares Weisse. “It’s extra important because it is shown more or less in the opening scene, with the curtains opening, like a theater, and the character in his bed. You’re discovering that he seems to live in a mansion, and then you have this beautiful view outside. We shot this model and the background was then added digitally. Because of what unfolds, you also see this model playing as a prop in the film.”

Indeed, Weisse got to have a cameo behind this model during the film. “That was fun. Alejandro used some of the people who were working on his film to play very small parts. I was with a model maker colleague in London, and we were just behind this model pretending to work as model makers on the model.”

The nature vista miniature was built as a forced perspective model, however, Weisse notes it was not intended to be crafted at a precise scale, and was a mix of scales. “It was about four meters wide and four meters deep, with between 12th and 24th scale at the front, and going back to be mountains at the back.”

The vista includes a large array of trees, which Weise originally thought could be fashioned from model railway trees. “Well, they always look a bit like plastic trees. So instead we used natural materials. Sometimes we go out in the field, in the forest, to try and find real things. We use branches and everything to put a structure to it. I mean, I had people building those trees for weeks and months.”

A level of atmosphere plays over the nature vista. This was orchestrated by Dominic Tuohy. “For that,” explains Weisse, “he used a water-based foam. We hadn’t used that before, so my big fear was that it changes the painted colors of the trees. But, no, it worked. The river was done in resin and I was also worried the foam would leave drops, but with the technique Dominic uses, there are no water drops. He did amazing work.”

Crafting an ice shelf

For the miniature ice shelf that is depicted heading towards Europe, the miniatures unit first referenced a real life iceberg called Iceberg A23a that had dislodged from Antarctica. “We found a lot of pictures of this iceberg on the internet,” notes Weisse. “Alejandro also went there to see it and photograph it. In the end, there was a big discussion how to do this iceberg. It had to look a bit menacing, a bit evil, but at the same time it had to look nice. Again, it had to play as an actual miniature for the visual effects and then appear as a prop in the movie.”

In terms of how the iceberg was created, Weisse says it was a tricky build. “Technically we couldn’t use simple polystyrene, because at that scale it had to be so fine. So we found a very, very fine foam. Very fine and very expensive! I had two sculptors who had a feeling for these natural things and they sculpted it with so much detail. That helped to make it alive.”

Some planes that are shown above the iceberg—and elsewhere—started life as miniatures. Weisse’s team made a B-2 Spirit bomber and other planes were built by The Magic Camera Company. Ultimately, says Weisse, ILM scanned the miniature planes and used Gaussian splatting techniques to replicate them for shots. “When they photographed and scanned them this way, you got every detail. You have the paint, the patina. It’s just amazing. For me, this new technique is so interesting because it’s a bit of a comeback for models and miniatures. It’s easier to use that Gaussian splatting scanning technique than to have to build the whole thing in CG to begin with. I mean, we also built the bomb that has ‘Suck it nature’ on it and a rig for it to fall. It was too complicated to film so they scanned that and did that digitally.” 

Views of the oil extraction activities on the original ice shelf were also realized with miniatures, including a remote-control model vehicle. “The landscape was forced perspective,” describes Weisse. “We had two scales because there were buildings and fences. In the foreground we had one scale, 25th scale, and in the background, to get a deepness, it was in 50th scale. The whole thing was 12 meters long. There’s a vehicle on there that was an RC toy I ordered on Amazon. Then I had one of my guys transform this vehicle. Sometimes we build this from scratch, sometimes we just use stuff we find and we transform it.”

Making the formal garden

Another miniature created by Weisse and his model makers was one they called the formal garden. This was inspired by a real location north of London called Tyringham. Miniature greenery and fog was another hallmark of the setup. It was also set on fire and burnt. 

In the centre of the garden is a water feature. For that, glass painted from below was used to stand in for the water. As with the opening nature vista, Weisse was adamant that real water would not work if incorporated with the miniature. “Real water doesn’t look right at the scale. I think the scale where you can have water in a miniature is third scale or fourth scale, and that’s the limit. Otherwise, it looks strange. If you have any movement on the water, it doesn’t look real. And if you have a drop somewhere, that drop would look huge and over-exaggerated. 

The scope of miniatures

Additional miniatures made for Digger included views of the European parliament, an oil rig, Rockwell’s private plane, and a ‘fake’ tree that topples outside a window, exposing that the story is actually a stage rehearsal. 

As noted, the models were created in Weisse’s Berlin studio then shipped via trucks to the UK. “We are very used to shipping them elsewhere,” advises Weisse. “We always build them in parts and we don’t do crates. We build shelves in the truck and just put the pieces on the shelves. That’s the most safe and secure way to ship them to London. You know, with crates, you can write ‘Fragile’ on them, but it doesn’t help.”

The miniatures were then reassembled for filming at Pinewood. They were shot digitally by Lubezki and incorporated into the film, which had been filmed in VistaVision. Weisse marvels at the lighting of the miniatures work, which included the use of LED screens for interactive lighting. “For example, on the nature vista, there was a huge LED panel on top with clouds going over. That gave a very interesting light on the model itself. It was Chivo’s idea to pretend that clouds are in the sky, so you had a difference of light on the model. That was new for me and it worked really well. I also asked for some shots of that to be done at 96 frames a second with the fog coming in. If you shoot miniatures with a higher speed, it can just look better.”

For Weisse, the opportunity to again contribute miniatures work to a major feature was a delight, especially for a film that features miniatures in a very meta way. “You know, 30 years ago, I thought miniatures were done in the movies. But with this film and others, they are coming back. There’s a return of this technique. And I think, mixed together with new technologies, it provides another form of art in the movies.”

entry.content:
Issue #70 of befores & afters magazine covers the visual effects of Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

DIGITAL MAGAZINE members can download the issue right now from the shop post.

With Spider-Man: Brand New Day, director Destin Daniel Cretton takes Peter Parker (Tom Holland) into a new chapter of his life, one that finds the web-slinger fighting crime full-time in a New York City that has forgotten his identity. As Peter grapples with the isolation of his new existence, an unexpected transformation threatens to change his abilities, while a seemingly new adversary in Jean Grey (Sadie Sink) appears to put the city and those Peter cares about in danger.

Bringing this world to the screen required a substantial visual effects effort, with production visual effects supervisor Jerome Chen and production visual effects producer David Masure-Bosco overseeing work across a number of facilities, including Sony Pictures Imageworks, Framestore and Industrial Light & Magic. Digital Domain and Torchlight contributed visualization services.

Several swinging sequences required particularly close attention to city builds and CG digi-doubles, as well as integrating live-action footage, physical effects and practical stunts into the final shots. Hulk (Mark Ruffalo) also features in the film, and was realized as a CG character. Finally, Jean Grey’s telekinetic mind wave abilities were ones that required visual effects design and execution, too. In this special issue of befores & afters magazine, we break down all the major effects sequences in Brand New Day with Chen and representatives from the VFX vendors.

entry.summary: A deep dive into the creatures this season. Today on the befores & afters podcast, we’re chatting about season 3 of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. I am joined by production visual effects supervisor Jason Smith. We do a deep dive into the Balrog revealed this season,
entry.content:
A deep dive into the creatures this season.

Today on the befores & afters podcast, we’re chatting about season 3 of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. I am joined by production visual effects supervisor Jason Smith.

We do a deep dive into the Balrog revealed this season, voiced by Simon Pegg. We talk about the design, the animation tests, the interaction with Charlie Vickers as Sauron, and the final VFX work by ILM. We also discuss other creatures – the Fell beast by DNEG and the Mûmakil by Rodeo FX. And we go into the ring forging sequence, which was handled by DNEG, plus a look at practical prosthetic effects for the Orcs by Barrie Gower’s team.

This is a fun chat, with spoilers if you haven’t watched the final eps of season 3.
